title: The seven practices, the PID and the project log
blurb: Name the seven practices and their purposes, and explain what the PID and the project log are for.
question: A team asks where the agreed direction and scope of the project are written down, and where today's issues and risks are recorded. Which two containers should the project manager point to?

teach.h: Seven practices, applied all the way through
teach.body: Formally: the seven practices describe essential aspects of project management that must be applied consistently throughout the project lifecycle. They are business case, organizing, plans, quality, risk, issues and progress. In plain English: these are the jobs that never stop. Every stage, someone is checking the project is still worth it, who does what, what gets built, how good it must be, what could go wrong, what has changed and where things stand.

teach.h: The seven practices at a glance
head: Practice
Purpose in brief
Memory hook
rows: Define products and the means to deliver them
User's requirements and how they will be met
Assess issues, control changes to baselines
Compare actual with plan, forecast, control
teach.caption: Each practice chapter follows the same pattern: purpose, guidance, technique, tailoring, management products, roles, links to the principles.

teach.body: The PID gives the direction and scope of the project and, together with the stage plan, forms the 'contract' between the project manager and the project board. It is an aggregation of management products created or updated during initiation and used to gain authorization. The authorized version is baselined, and at closure actual performance is compared against it in the end project report.

The project log is the dynamic record of the project. It holds six records: the daily log, the lessons log, and the issue, risk, quality and product registers. The daily log and lessons log are started in starting up a project, the log is completed in initiation, and it is closed in closing a project. Think of the PID as the agreed plan of record and the project log as the running diary.

teach.h: What each project log record holds
head: Record
Holds
rows: Informal or sensitive issues, notes, actions
Lessons from this and earlier projects
All products of a plan and their status
teach.caption: Initial risks found in starting up go in the daily log until the risk register exists.

rows.label: Main use
values: Recording what happens day to day

teach.h: Which container does this belong in?
teach.caption: Procedures live in the management approaches in the PID; the specific risks and issues live in the registers.

teach.body: Kestrel Valley Water is replacing its meter-reading system. In initiation, project manager Priya Okafor pulls the full business case, project plan, management approaches and project controls into the PID for board approval. Meanwhile she logs a supplier's informal worry in the daily log, a formal request for change in the issue register and a new threat in the risk register. When the board authorizes the project, the PID is baselined; the registers keep growing every week.

teach.text: Classic trap: mixing up the approach with the register. The risk management approach (part of the PID) holds the procedure, scales and responsibilities; the risk register (part of the project log) holds the specific risks. The same split applies to issues and quality. Second trap: the PID is assembled in initiating a project, not in starting up; the project brief is the starting up product.

items: Seven practices: business case, organizing, plans, quality, risk, issues, progress.
They are applied consistently throughout the project lifecycle.
PID: direction and scope; with the stage plan, the 'contract' between PM and board; baselined when authorized.
Project log: daily log, lessons log, issue, risk, quality and product registers.
Project log started in starting up, completed in initiation, closed in closing a project.

summary: You can now name the seven practices and state each purpose in brief. You can also explain why the PID is the baselined basis for authorizing the project while the project log is the dynamic record of what happens.

A.q: Which practice has the purpose of collecting and assessing issues and controlling changes to the project's baseline?
A.why: The issues practice collects and assesses issues and controls changes to the baseline; in PRINCE2 7 it includes change control (manual 10.1).

whyNot.0: Progress compares actual achievement with the plan, forecasts and controls deviations.
whyNot.1: Risk identifies, assesses and controls uncertainties.
whyNot.3: Quality documents the user's requirements and how they will be met.

A.q: What is the purpose of the project initiation documentation (PID)?
options: To record informal issues and actions day to day
To give the direction and scope of the project
To provide a firm foundation for initiation
To summarize stage status for the project board
A.why: The PID gives the direction and scope of the project and, with the stage plan, forms the 'contract' between the project manager and the board (manual 4.3.1).

whyNot.0: Informal issues and actions go in the daily log, part of the project log.
whyNot.2: A full and firm foundation for initiation is the purpose of the project brief.
whyNot.3: A summary of stage status for the board is a highlight report.

A.q: Which records make up the project log?
options: Daily log, lessons log, issue and risk registers, and the PID
Issue, risk and quality registers, and the management approaches
Lessons log, issue register, risk register and highlight reports
Daily log, lessons log, issue, risk, quality and product registers
A.why: The project log holds six records: daily log, lessons log, and the issue, risk, quality and product registers (manual 4.3.2).

whyNot.0: The PID is a separate container; it is not part of the project log.
whyNot.1: The management approaches sit in the PID, not the project log.
whyNot.2: Highlight reports are progress reports to the board, not project log records.

B.q:
Which two statements about the PID and the project log are correct?
1. The PID, with the stage plan, forms the 'contract' between the project manager and the project board.
2. The project log is baselined when the project is authorized.
3. The project log holds six records, including the quality register.
4. The PID is assembled in starting up a project.
B.why: Statement 1 matches manual 4.3.1 and statement 3 matches 4.3.2: the project log holds the daily log, lessons log and four registers, one of which is the quality register.

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: the PID is baselined; the project log is a dynamic record.
whyNot.2: Both are false: the log is not baselined, and the PID is assembled in initiating a project.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: starting up produces the project brief; the PID is assembled in initiation.

B.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. The [?] practice defines and establishes the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities.
B.why: The organizing practice defines and establishes the structure of accountability and responsibilities: the 'who' (manual 6.1).

whyNot.1: Plans define the products and the means to deliver them.
whyNot.2: Progress monitors actual achievement against the plan and controls deviations.
whyNot.3: Business case judges whether the project is desirable, viable and achievable.

B.q: The senior user mentions a sensitive concern in a corridor conversation and asks for it to be kept informal for now. Where should the project manager record it?
B.why: Informal or sensitive issues are recorded in the daily log, part of the project log.

whyNot.0: The issue register holds formal issues that are being managed through the issue procedure.
whyNot.1: The lessons log holds lessons that could help this or future projects.
whyNot.3: The risk management approach holds procedures and scales, not individual concerns.

C.q: In which process is the PID assembled, and what happens to the version used to gain authorization?
options: Initiating a project; it is baselined
Starting up a project; it is baselined
Initiating a project; it is archived
Managing a stage boundary; it is closed
C.why: The PID is assembled in initiating a project, and the version used to gain authorization is baselined and placed under change control (manual 15.4.6).

whyNot.1: Starting up assembles the project brief, not the PID.
whyNot.2: The process is right, but the authorized PID is baselined, not archived; archiving happens at closure.
whyNot.3: Stage boundaries review and may update the PID; they do not assemble or close it.

C.q: Which practice's purpose includes forecasting the project's objectives and continued viability, and what cycle is it based on?
C.why: The progress practice monitors actual against planned achievement, provides a forecast for objectives and continued viability, and controls deviations; it is based on a plan-do-check-act cycle (manual 11.1).

whyNot.0: Plans define the products and the means to deliver them; they do not provide the forecast against tolerances.
whyNot.1: Risk controls uncertainty; forecasting objectives against the plan is progress.
whyNot.2: The business case judges desirability, viability and achievability; the forecast mechanism is progress.

C.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the PID from the project log?
options: The PID holds the registers; the log holds the approaches
The PID is set up in starting up; the log is built in initiation
The PID is a baselined basis for approval; the log is a running record
The PID is updated daily; the log is reviewed at stage boundaries
C.why: The PID is the baselined basis for authorizing the project; the project log is the dynamic record of logs and registers.

whyNot.0: It is the other way round: approaches are in the PID, registers are in the project log.
whyNot.1: The project log is started in starting up; the PID is assembled in initiation.
whyNot.3: The project log is updated continually; the PID is reviewed and updated at stage boundaries.

reteach.title: The signed agreement and the notebook
reteach.question: If you hired a builder, which would you keep in a folder and which in a notebook: the signed agreement on what will be built, or the notes of each day's problems?

blocks.body: The signed agreement says what is being done, why, how it will be controlled and at what cost. You only change it formally. That is the PID. The notebook records each day's events: a worry raised, a lesson learned, a risk spotted, a check passed, a product finished. That is the project log, with its daily log, lessons log and four registers.

blocks.text: Approaches (procedures) go in the PID; registers (the actual risks, issues, quality checks and products) go in the project log.

explain.body: Business case (why), organizing (who), plans (what, how, when, how much), quality, risk, issues and progress. Each is applied consistently throughout the project lifecycle.

test.q: Which practice defines the 'who' of the project?
test.why: Organizing defines the structure of accountability and responsibilities: the 'who'.

whyNot.2: Progress monitors and controls actual achievement against plans.
whyNot.3: Business case covers the 'why': whether the project is desirable, viable and achievable.

explain.body: Gives the direction and scope of the project. With the stage plan it forms the 'contract' between the project manager and the board. It is assembled in initiation and baselined when authorized.

test.q: Which product, together with the stage plan, forms the 'contract' between the project manager and the project board?
test.why: The PID, with the stage plan, forms the 'contract' between the project manager and the board (manual 4.3.1).

whyNot.0: The project brief is the foundation for initiation; it is superseded by the PID.
whyNot.2: The business case is one part of the PID, not the 'contract' itself.
whyNot.3: The project plan is one part of the PID, not the 'contract' itself.

explain.h: Six records in the project log
explain.body: Daily log, lessons log, issue register, risk register, quality register and product register. The quality register tracks quality activities; the product register tracks every product of a plan and its status.

test.q: Which project log record holds the status of all the products in a plan?
test.why: The product register lists the products of a plan and their status.

whyNot.0: The quality register records planned quality activities and their results.
whyNot.1: The issue register records formal issues.
whyNot.2: The daily log records informal issues, notes and actions.

explain.body: The daily log and lessons log are started in starting up a project. The rest of the project log is set up in initiation. The project log is closed in closing a project.

test.q: In which process is the project log closed?
test.why: Preparing planned closure includes closing the project log, in closing a project.

whyNot.0: Stage boundaries review registers but do not close the project log.
whyNot.2: The board authorizes closure in directing a project; the PM closes the log in closing a project.
whyNot.3: Controlling a stage keeps the log up to date during the stage.
